clue.text: 12 × 24 Heather finds trivial

blocks.note: 12 is the grid's ROMAN NUMERAL entry and 24 is INCH, so the sum reads twelve inches, a unit of length
ling is the common heather plant

explanation.surface: Someone studying a sum and a sprig of heather and dismissing them as unimportant.
explanation.walkthrough: The multiplication sign is not maths to do but a measurement to name: take the entries at 12 and 24 literally, as twelve inches, giving FOOT, then add LING.
explanation.definitionFit: Footling is an informal British adjective for petty, unimportant, of no real consequence.

clue.text: Most unclear as Post Office rejected an inquiry

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back the way it came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation for Post Office
the indefinite article shortened
a quest is a search or investigation

explanation.surface: A complaint about bureaucracy: the Post Office turned down a query and left things murkier than ever.
explanation.walkthrough: OPAQUEST is the superlative of opaque, built as OP + A + QUEST.
explanation.definitionFit: Opaque means not transparent or hard to understand, so the superlative form is the least clear of all.

clue.text: Top secret number – good feature for TV gameshow

blocks.note: the tip of something is its top
a PIN is the secret code number for a bank card
G is the usual abbreviation for good
a point is a feature or characteristic, as in 'one of its good points'

explanation.surface: A quiz producer describing a top-secret code number as a good gimmick for a game show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top secret' reads as one phrase but must be split after its first word. Tipping Point is a long-running British ITV quiz built around a coin-pushing machine.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer names a specific British television quiz programme, so the definition gives its category rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Grass doing well

blocks.note: first meaning: a verb in British slang, to tell tales to the police
second meaning: read as two words, playing or performing at one's best

explanation.walkthrough: Grass looks like lawn doing nicely; in British slang to grass is to tell the police about someone. Split the answer as IN FORM for the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To inform on someone is to betray them to authorities, and being in form means performing at a high standard.

clue.text: Mistake giving new order to "about turn"

indicators.note: putting the quoted words in a new order means the two-word phrase is read back to front, word by word

blocks.note: a turn in a game is a go
of can mean about, as in 'speak of the devil'

explanation.surface: A drill sergeant's blunder in calling out an about-turn the wrong way round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About turn' looks like a single reversal instruction, but it is the fodder: swap its two words to get 'turn about', then translate each, GO + OF.
explanation.definitionFit: A goof is an informal word for a silly error or blunder.

clue.text: Intensity of keeping fit in climbing centre – quite the reverse close to holiday

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means going upwards, so the letters read bottom to top
to keep something is to hold it within, so one piece goes inside another
this says the holding runs the opposite way from what was just stated, so swap which piece is inside
the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is taken

blocks.note: taken as written
the core of something is its centre
the final letter of holiday

explanation.surface: A gym-goer describing the intensity of keeping fit at a climbing centre right up to their holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, the clue puts the fitness word inside the climbing one; 'quite the reverse' swaps that, so the climbing centre sits inside, with the holiday's last letter at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Ferocity is fierceness or great force, so it serves as a synonym for intensity of feeling or action.

clue.text: Trouble Smee discovered on ship

indicators.note: dis-covered means with its covering taken off, so the outer letters go and the inside stays
in a down entry, one thing on another sits above it, so the first piece is placed on top

blocks.note: the inside letters of the name once its first and last letters are stripped
SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: A Peter Pan scene: Captain Hook's bosun Smee is found aboard the Jolly Roger and is in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' seems to mean found, but it means uncovered: stripping Smee's outer letters. Smee is Captain Hook's sidekick in Peter Pan.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a mess means being in difficulty, so the noun serves as a synonym for a predicament.

clue.text: Street getting louder – sounds like tea party is scrapped

indicators.note: something scrapped is thrown away, so these letters are removed from the word
this tells us to use a letter that is pronounced the same as the word

blocks.note: the musical term for a gradual increase in volume
a do is a party; these letters are taken out
the letter's name is pronounced like the drink

explanation.surface: A complaint about a street getting noisier and noisier, until the neighbours' tea party is cancelled.
explanation.walkthrough: Take CRESCENDO, scrap the party DO to leave CRESCEN, then add T, the letter that sounds like 'tea'.
explanation.definitionFit: A crescent is a curved residential road, and many British street names end in the word.

clue.text: Accidentally catch 6 balls – then try

blocks.note: in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled from one end
a judge tries or hears a case in court

explanation.surface: A cricket fielder taking an accidental catch in an over, then having another go.
explanation.walkthrough: In a puzzle full of cross-references, '6' looks like a pointer to 6 Down; here it is just the number six. 'Catch' is the sense of catching words, not a ball.
explanation.definitionFit: To overhear is to pick up words not meant for you, which is catching speech by accident.

clue.text: Bringing in expert obviously, checks building regs require them

indicators.note: to bring something in is to take it inside, so the following pieces are placed within another

blocks.note: to restrain or check, as in lessening enthusiasm or muffling a piano string's vibration
a pro is a professional, an expert
'of course' means naturally, obviously

explanation.surface: A builder grumbling that the regulations demand an expert's checks, as if that were obvious.
explanation.walkthrough: The containing word comes last in the clue, so read it first and fit the rest inside. Building regs are the UK Building Regulations, the rules new buildings must meet.
explanation.definitionFit: A damp-proof course is a waterproof layer laid in a wall near ground level, mandated by construction rules to stop rising moisture.

clue.text: See 10
For example, I translated Norman Mailer after I left university

indicators.note: translating turns words into a new form, so these letters are rearranged
once one letter has departed, another arrives in its place

blocks.note: the American novelist's name, taken as letters
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A student translated Norman Mailer's novels after leaving university.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'I' of the surface is a letter: take the I out of NORMAN MAILER, put U in, and rearrange. The definition's 'I' is the numeral one.
explanation.definitionFit: The letter I represents the number one in the Roman system, so it is one instance of the category named.

clue.text: View page about German writer backing Twain and Orwell?

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps round the next
going backwards means the whole thing is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: to view is to see
P is the standard abbreviation for page
Thomas Mann, the German novelist

explanation.surface: A reader looking up a page about a German author, while preferring Twain and Orwell.
explanation.walkthrough: Build the view-plus-page word around the novelist, then read the whole thing backwards. The question mark flags a definition by example: both writers used assumed names.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Twain and George Orwell were pseudonyms of Samuel Clemens and Eric Blair, so both are examples of authors' assumed names.

clue.text: Film succeeded, one getting a lot of laughs

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for succeeded, as in genealogies

blocks.clueFragment: one getting a lot of laughs
blocks.note: a hoot is a very funny person or thing

explanation.surface: A comedy film was a success, its star drawing lots of laughs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' looks like a noun, the comedy in question, but it is the verb: to film is to shoot.
explanation.definitionFit: To shoot a scene is to film it with a camera, a standard sense in cinema.

clue.text: Convict popular couple

blocks.note: something in is fashionable or popular
to couple animals is to mate them

explanation.surface: A court verdict against a well-liked couple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Convict' looks like a verb, as in a court convicting the couple; it is the noun, a prisoner.
explanation.definitionFit: An inmate is someone held in prison, and a convict is a person serving a sentence there.

clue.text: Cease work on street

indicators.note: in an across entry, one thing on another comes after it, so the first piece named goes second

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street
op is short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: An order to halt the roadworks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work on street' sounds like roadworks; OP is the crossword abbreviation for opus, a work.
explanation.definitionFit: To stop is to come to an end or halt, a direct synonym of the verb cease.

clue.text: Making Law Reform Institute pens dependable

indicators.note: to reform something is to reshape it, so these letters take a new arrangement
to pen is to enclose, so one piece is shut inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
to institute something is to start it

explanation.surface: A Law Reform Institute drafting rules that are reliable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Law Reform Institute' reads as one body's name, but 'Institute' is a verb meaning START and 'Reform' is the anagram signal for LAW.
explanation.definitionFit: Stalwart describes someone loyal, reliable and hard-working, so it is a synonym for trustworthy and steady.

clue.text: Literary work – first to satirise politician

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A satirical novel whose first aim is to lampoon a politician.
explanation.walkthrough: Tory is the everyday name for a British Conservative, a stock crossword politician.
explanation.definitionFit: A story is a narrative, an example of imaginative writing in prose.

clue.text: Vocally support processed pork, safe

indicators.note: processed food is broken down and remade, so these letters are reworked

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A food-safety campaigner vocally backing processed pork as safe to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Processed pork' reads as luncheon meat, but 'processed' is the anagram signal working on 'pork, safe'.
explanation.definitionFit: To speak for someone is to argue on their behalf or represent their view out loud.

clue.text: Comfortable home is part of Crown Estate

indicators.note: being part of something means sitting within it, so the letters lie inside the phrase

blocks.note: the letters run consecutively across the two words

explanation.surface: A cosy residence that belongs to the Crown Estate, the royal property portfolio.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles crowN ESTate. The Crown Estate is the British monarch's property holding, including many grand homes.
explanation.definitionFit: A nest is a cosy, snug home, used figuratively for a comfortable place to live.

clue.text: Didn't leave guy swelling up

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a guy or stay is a rope that steadies a mast or tent
a node is a small swelling or lump

explanation.surface: A man stuck around despite his swelling coming up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' looks like a man but it is the rope sense, a stay.
explanation.definitionFit: To stay on is to remain somewhere rather than depart, so it matches the negated verb phrase.

clue.text: Andy regularly failing to get guidance

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the first and third letters
a vice is a moral failing or weakness

explanation.surface: Andy keeps failing and needs someone to guide him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Failing' reads as a verb, Andy failing; it is the noun, a weakness.
explanation.definitionFit: Advice is counsel offered to help someone decide what to do, the same as guidance.

clue.text: Court tense – ultimately you arraign almost all bawdy houses

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so the last letters of the next words are taken
nearly the whole of something means it falls one letter short
to house something is to give it room inside, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense
ribald means coarse or bawdy
the final letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A tense courtroom where, in the end, you charge nearly every brothel keeper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bawdy houses' reads as brothels, but 'houses' is a verb: RIBAL(D), short of its last letter, houses UN, all after T.
explanation.definitionFit: A tribunal is a body that sits in judgment on disputes, a kind of court.

clue.text: Way to print degenerate joke, wasting a couple of seconds

indicators.note: to waste something is to lose it, so these letters are thrown out

blocks.note: to sink is to decline or degenerate
a jest is a joke
S is the abbreviation for second; two of them are removed

explanation.surface: Advice on how to publish a filthy joke, after losing a few seconds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Degenerate joke' looks like a dirty joke but splits into a verb and a noun, and each word sheds a single S.
explanation.definitionFit: Inkjet printing sprays tiny droplets onto paper, one of the common methods home printers use.

clue.text: Damage wrecked Hulk tie-in rollercoaster?

indicators.note: damaging something knocks it out of shape, so these letters are broken up and rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A theme-park ride tied in with the Hulk film has been wrecked by damage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrecked' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder; 'Damage' at the front does the work. The question mark marks a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A rollercoaster is the classic thrilling fairground attraction, so frightening that riders grip until their knuckles go pale.

clue.text: Creep home before church

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming before means sitting higher, so the first piece goes on top

blocks.note: to be in is to be at home
CH is the abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: Someone sneaking home just before the church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creep' looks like a noun, an unpleasant person; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To inch along is to move very slowly by small degrees, which is creeping.

clue.text: Employed and happy but not in the morning

indicators.note: 'but not' excludes what follows, so those letters are dropped

blocks.note: amused means entertained, happy
AM stands for ante meridiem, before noon; these letters are dropped

explanation.surface: Someone who has a job and is cheerful, except first thing in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Employed' reads as having a job; here it means put to use. AMUSED loses AM.
explanation.definitionFit: Used and employed both mean put to service or applied for a purpose.

clue.text: See 23
Shock, with pacifist on flyer

blocks.note: to rock someone is to shake or shock them
in politics a dove favours peace over war

explanation.surface: A peace campaigner gets a fright on board an aeroplane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flyer' suggests a passenger or leaflet; it is a bird. The rock dove is the wild ancestor of the town pigeon.
explanation.definitionFit: A rock dove is a wild pigeon species, and any bird can be called a flyer in crosswords.

clue.text: Glib words after tryst? There's a time and place for this

definitions.text: There's a time and place for this

indicators.note: coming after something means being placed behind it, so the first piece named goes second

blocks.note: a tryst is a romantic meeting
a line is a smooth, practised patter, as in a chat-up line

explanation.surface: Smooth talk following a romantic meeting, with the warning that such things have their proper moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'There's a time and place for this' sounds like a rebuke; read literally, it describes a newspaper heading that gives when and where a story was filed.
explanation.definitionFit: A dateline is the line at the top of a news report stating the place and date it was written.
